body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Five camp talks for Tobin, about how Tobin feels about the party and about the road. The talks that depend on how the party treats Tobin are not about any deed in particular. The companion is TOBIN HAYWARD (call them Tobin in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these five talks, in this order, with these keys. Every talk is a private word at the fire in a different mood. Do not repeat a topic across them.

TALK strained. Tobin has lost faith in the party: the party's choices have drifted away from what Tobin holds dear (read the note's "Approval moments" for what they like and dislike). Do not claim a specific deed; speak of "the way things have gone" and name what Tobin cares about. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row (where they sit: apart from the fire, what their hands are doing), then 3 or 4 SAY rows saying what is wrong, in their own voice, stern and hurt, not shouting. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (listens, owns it, asks them to say what would mend it); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies: 1 reply row each for the cold one, 2 rows for the good one.

TALK doubt. Tobin is doubtful: not angry, but they have doubts about how the party goes about things. Gentler than strained, more puzzled and wary. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (takes the doubt seriously and asks what they would do differently); OPTION 2 answers coldly (a flip remark that brushes the doubt off); OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows for the other two, each with a REASON row.

TALK act1. The first night in Wickermoor, a few hours after the Ghostlight Express crashed. Tobin is still shaken and in their own way trying to be useful. They talk about the crash, the Hollow, the endless night and the Crooked Moon through their own eyes (their trade, their habits, their fears from the note), not about plot. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (a second NARRATOR row is allowed). Three options: OPTION 1 asks how they are holding up; OPTION 2 shares something of the party's own; OPTION 3 says they should get some rest and leaves it there. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act2. Deep in the troubles of the Hollow: the party has been through a lot and Tobin has seen the party fight, win and lose. Something small has shifted in how Tobin sees these people. Keep to the Hollow in general: name no place and no event except the Crooked House (the haunted manor on the hill, already cleansed) and the crash. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles as act1. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act3. The last stretch has begun; whatever is coming is close, and everyone knows it. Tobin is weary, truthful and a little funny about it, and says something about what the road has made of them and the party. Name no place and no event except the Hollow in general. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: strained, doubt, act1, act2, act3.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/tobin_hayward-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for TOBIN HAYWARD (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Tobin likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/tobin_hayward-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Tobin, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK strained
NARRATOR: Tobin sits on an upturned crate well back from the firelight, scraping dry mud from his pruning knife with a thumb of stiff burlap.
SAY: I have kept a clean ledger all my life, and I do not care for the entries we have been making lately.
SAY: Throwing live sparks near dry brush, writing off sick ground that could still be mended, leaving hurt creatures to rot in the ditch.
SAY: That is not field surgery, that is plain butchery, and I did not stitch my boots on to walk behind a blight.
SAY: If we are only here to scorch what looks ugly, you and I are going to have a very short season together.
OPTION 1: You're right. Tell me how we set the ledger straight.
OPTION 2: The valley is ugly, Tobin. We do what works.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: Start by minding your sparks and tending what can still draw breath instead of kicking the taproot out.
SAY: Keep your hands steady on the next row, and we will see if the soil holds.
REASON: You listened when I called you out on our work.
REPLY 2
SAY: Any fool with a torch can clear an acre, and all he gets for his trouble is a mouthful of ash.
REASON: You brushed off my warning at the fire.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Tobin slides the knife back into his belt and pulls his hat low, watchin' the dark beyond the trees.
SAY: Aye, well, keep your boots out of the embers before you turn in.
TALK doubt
NARRATOR: Tobin squats three paces from the fire with a bundle of dry rushes across his knees, twisting a splint and pulling the knot too tight.
SAY: I have been watching the way we move through this parish, and the stitchwork is getting sloppy.
SAY: Half the time we charge through the rows like stray cattle, wasting good herbs and leaving bruised stems behind us.
SAY: You cannot cure a rot if you do not stop to read the bark first.
OPTION 1: Fair point. How would you have us work the next stretch?
OPTION 2: We're alive, aren't we? Save the lecture for the crops.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: Slower on the approach, quieter with the lanterns, and we salvage what timber and medicine the ruins leave us.
SAY: A tidy camp keeps the pulse steady when the hexing thickens.
REASON: You asked how I would mend our pace.
REPLY 2
SAY: Alive for today, maybe, though a frayed seam always parts when the frost bites hardest.
REASON: You laughed off my doubts about the road.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: A field-mouse pokes its nose from Tobin's lapel, and he taps it gently back into his pocket with a wooden finger.
SAY: Sleep while you can, then, I will finish sorting these rushes myself.
TALK act1
NARRATOR: Tobin sits on a dry stone three paces from the fire, pluckin' splinters of train-car oak out of his burlap knees.
SAY: Hold still, you're fraying at the cuff and your collar has got half a window-frame tangled in the hem.
SAY: Never mind, that is my own sleeve I am looking at, my eyes are still rattling from the rails.
SAY: One minute we are rolling through the fog, and the next the whole carriage pitches into the ditch like an overturned hay-wain.
NARRATOR: He tips his head back toward the crone-faced moon, one wooden hand resting over the turnip-lantern cold against his collarbone.
SAY: Look at that sour old face up there, staring down like a bailiff over a bad harvest.
SAY: No dawn coming to dry the dew, just damp soil that smells of fifty-year canker and wet iron.
SAY: My mice have not stopped shivering since the boiler burst, and I had to evict a cinder the size of a walnut from my hatband.
SAY: Still, the ribs held, the herb satchel stayed dry, and nobody here has split a main seam yet.
OPTION 1: Never mind our cuffs. How are you holding up after that wreck?
OPTION 2: None of us expected to wake up under that moon.
OPTION 3: Put the needle away and get some rest, Tobin.
REPLY 1
SAY: Dry and intact, which is all a straw man can ask after flying through a baggage door.
SAY: Give me an hour to re-tie my left wrist and I will be ready to inspect the parish.
REASON: You asked how I held up after the crash.
REPLY 2
SAY: Aye, well, when you are dropped in a strange orchard in the dark, you check the roots at your boots first.
SAY: We will take the measure of that moon once we have the camp in order.
REASON: You shared a quiet word on our first night.
REPLY 3
SAY: Rest is for people whose stuffing does not shift when they roll over.
SAY: Go on to your bedroll, I will keep an eye on the sparks until the wood settles.
REASON: You told me to rest after the crash.
TALK act2
NARRATOR: Tobin sits on a dry root with his herb satchel open between his boots, sorting bundles of fever-bark by the light of the fire.
SAY: When we walked down from the Crooked House with the glass still ringing in our ears, I figured this lot would come apart at the first hard frost.
SAY: Too much noise, too many loose threads, and not one of you knows how to walk past a bramble without snagging a cloak.
SAY: Instead we have been knee-deep in every sour ditch in Wickermoor Hollow, and you are all still standing on your own two feet.
SAY: You take a blow, you bleed a little sap, and then you tie the rag tight and step right back into the row.
SAY: Good soil, bad seed, I used to say, and I was sure this valley had nothing left in it worth grafting.
SAY: Now I catch myself counting four pulses every ten minutes just to make sure the ledger has not gone short.
SAY: Do not let it go to your head, mind, your posture is still dreadful.
OPTION 1: And how is the surgeon holding up under all this mud?
OPTION 2: We only keep standing because you keep stitching us back together.
OPTION 3: Get some rest, Tobin. The ledger looks fine tonight.
REPLY 1
SAY: Damp around the ankles and running low on clean linen thread, if you want the honest tally.
SAY: Still, the core straw is dry, and the work beats sitting on a fence post.
REASON: You checked on me deep in the Hollow.
REPLY 2
SAY: Sound husbandry, nothing more, it wastes less medicine if I catch the tear before it reaches the bone.
SAY: Though I will admit you lot make finer timber than I first marked you for.
REASON: You thanked me for keeping the party mended.
REPLY 3
SAY: Fine is a big word for a camp with three frayed hems and a dented kettle.
SAY: Go on and sleep, I am only waxing this twine before the damp gets in.
REASON: You sent me to bed with a steady word.
TALK act3
NARRATOR: The fire has burned down to low red coals, and Tobin sits closer than usual, turnin' a small braided rush ring between his fingers.
SAY: Listen to the wind coming down the Hollow tonight, thick as cellar-damp and twice as cold.
SAY: Whatever has been rotting at the taproot of this valley is just up the lane now, you can taste the iron on the tongue.
SAY: Funny thing is, my chest is not hammering the way it did the night the train came off the rails.
SAY: I spent my whole second life keeping three paces from every lantern, fussing over cuffs so I would not have to look at the ash.
SAY: Then I fell in with a pack of stubborn fools who walk straight into the dark and expect a straw man to keep up.
SAY: Whatever happens at the end of this row, I am glad my stitching held long enough to walk it with you.
SAY: Now wipe that look off your face before the mice think I have gone soft in the gourd.
OPTION 1: How are you feeling with the end of the road so close?
OPTION 2: We walked it together, Tobin. Nobody's stitching fails tonight.
OPTION 3: Rest up while the coals are low. Tomorrow will be heavy.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Tobin touches the front of his coat once, right over the dry rustle in his ribs, then drops his hand to his knee.
SAY: Lighter than I have been in a long time, and ready to see the bill paid in full.
SAY: Just keep your boots clear of the cinders when the work starts.
REASON: You asked how I felt before the last stretch.
REPLY 2
SAY: That is the spirit, clean knots and steady hands all the way to the boundary stone.
SAY: If the blight wants this parish, it will have to chew through some very tough burlap first.
REASON: You stood by me before the final stretch.
REPLY 3
SAY: Aye, even a field surgeon knows when to shut the ledger and save his breath.
SAY: Goodnight, friend, I will see you when the lanterns go up.
REASON: You bade me rest before the last fight.
